doc.title: Sonny Rollins — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Listening to his own recordings and the curse of many takes
summary: He finds judging his own recordings excruciating and says take after take at Fantasy Records did not help.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: There is a man who has collected many airchecks, soundchecks, recording of you over the years. What is his name? His name is Carl...something?

Smith, yeah. So, there’s this big treasure trove of your stuff, and clearly you listen to something in order to make a decision what to release. What is that process when you’re hearing yourself, how do you decide this is worth releasing...
...but this is not? But...take us through that process when you’re listening?
Well, because I’m a guy that–you’re talking about two things: first, you’re talking about music; now you’re talking about listening to myself.
Okay. Myself, I’m one of these guys that’s very conscious of anything I do that may be, that, you know, I’m a strict perfectionist.

So, I can hear something and I say, “Oh, god, why did I do that?” or, “Why didn’t that...?” This kind of stuff. So, it’s very difficult when I’m making a record uh...and I have to listen to myself. It’s really the hardest part in trying to figure out what is acceptable to me, and, therefore, may be acceptable to the public, you know. So, that’s, that’s rough. That’s, that’s, that’s rough.
When you’re in this...doing a studio session, do you generally go for first takes, or do you try and perfect it?

Well...yeah, no. I, I, many years ago when I first started recording, that technology was not available. So, it was only first takes, or maybe second takes, maybe, but that was it. There wasn’t a whole lot of takes. As years, technology advanced, then you had the–which was a curse to me, because then when I was, I remember I was at Fantasy [Records] and I used to do, we would just do take after take after take, you know, because I’m trying to get the perfect take. And it’s, it’s not going to happen. So, it became a very uh...you know, uh...I, I, I–the technology in that case didn’t work on my behalf.
